_comment: The bibliography behind every citation in core.json. The pack stores an identifier; this stores what the identifier IS, so a reader can see the paper without leaving the app. Every record here was resolved against CrossRef (or PubMed, or arXiv) and its title, journal, authors and year read off that record -- nothing is recalled, and nothing is added from a reference list without resolving it first. `year` is the issue year, which is what a reader will match against; several of these were online-first the year before. A record carries a `doi` OR a `pmid`: some journals issue no DOI at all, and refusing them would mean the pack could cite a paper no reader could ever be shown. One record is an arXiv preprint and says so in its journal and establishes fields -- it is here to attribute a widely quoted figure, not to support a claim, and nothing cites it. NO commercial organisation, product or certification body may be named in this file: core_pack_test greps content bytes for it, and two of these papers have manufacturer-employed authors -- they are peer-reviewed with DOIs, and only the work is recorded.

references.title: Low Back Pain in Professional Golfers: The Role of Associated Hip and Low Back Range-of-Motion Deficits
references.authors: Vad, Bhat, Basrai, Gebeh, Aspergren, Andrews
references.journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
references.establishes: In 42 male professional golfers, a history of low back pain correlated with decreased LEAD hip internal rotation, FABERE distance and lumbar extension. No significant trail-hip finding — the asymmetry is the result.

references.title: Lumbopelvic kinematic characteristics of golfers with limited hip rotation
references.journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
references.establishes: Golfers with hip internal rotation below 20° showed significantly greater lumbar flexion, axial rotation and lateral bending, and greater pelvic posterior tilt, than those at or above 30°.

references.title: Kinematic relationship between rotation of lumbar spine and hip joints during golf swing in professional golfers
references.establishes: Lumbar–hip rotational coupling of r≈0.81. The lead hip's contribution to overall rotation is markedly high in the EARLY downswing; the lumbar spine contributes more late.

references.title: The Biomechanics of the Modern Golf Swing: Implications for Lower Back Injuries
references.establishes: Review. Skilled golfers laterally slide the pelvis toward the target and this contributes to clubhead speed; argues the lumbar spine may not safely accommodate the resulting loads.

references.title: Low back pain and golf: A review of biomechanical risk factors
references.establishes: Professionals with low back pain show significantly more lead-side lateral bending in the backswing. Notes that crunch-factor evidence is conflicting and was not reproduced as a risk factor by two independent methods.

references.title: Biomechanical parameters of the golf swing associated with lower back pain: A systematic review
references.authors: Watson, Coughlan, Clement, Murray, Murray, Miller
references.establishes: Mixed and null results: NO significant differences in hip angle, trunk angle or crunch factor in recreational golfers. Elite golfers with low back pain showed shorter transition phases and greater peak lead-side lumbar lateral flexion. Nothing cites it, and it is the most load-bearing uncited paper here: it is the reason every injury note in the library is phrased as an association with stated uncertainty rather than as a risk, and no note may be strengthened past what it supports.

references.title: The role of upper torso and pelvis rotation in driving performance during the golf swing
references.authors: Myers, Lephart, Tsai, Sell, Smoliga, Jolly
references.establishes: X-factor and upper-torso rotational velocity are significantly related to ball velocity. Read alongside Madrid et al. 2020, which disagrees.

references.title: The relationship between biomechanical variables and driving performance during the golf swing
references.establishes: Models accounted for 44–74% of ball-velocity variance. X-factor, delayed release of the arms and wrists, trunk tilting and weight shifting were significantly related to ball velocity. Read alongside Madrid et al. 2020, which disagrees on wrist release.

references.title: Elite golfers' kinematic sequence in full-swing and partial-swing shots
references.establishes: Significant proximal-to-distal temporal sequencing with a successive increase in peak segment angular speed — across genders, skill levels, and both full and partial shots.

references.title: Rotational Biomechanics of the Elite Golf Swing: Benchmarks for Amateurs
references.authors: Meister, Ladd, Butler, Zhao, Rogers, Ray, Rose
references.establishes: 10 professional and 5 amateur male golfers. Benchmark curves for pelvic rotation, upper-torso rotation and X-factor across the whole swing. In professionals, peak free moment per kilogram, peak X-factor and peak S-factor were highly consistent — coefficients of variation 6.8%, 7.4% and 8.4%. The downswing was initiated by reversal of pelvic rotation followed by reversal of upper-torso rotation, and peak X-factor preceded peak free moment in every swing of every golfer, occurring during the initial downswing. For amateurs, the number of factors falling outside one to two standard deviations of the professional means increased with handicap.

references.title: Golf Swing Rotational Velocity: The Essential Follow-Through
references.authors: Steele, Roh, Mahtani, Meister, Ladd, Rose
references.establishes: 11 professionals compared with 5 amateurs. Rotational velocities were highly consistent in professionals through the downswing — coefficients of variation 0.086 for upper torso and 0.079 for pelvis. Peak upper-torso rotational velocity and peak X-prime occurred AFTER impact, in the follow-through, while peak pelvic rotational velocity occurred during the downswing. Pelvic velocity at impact was reduced in amateurs compared with professionals (p=0.019).

references.title: The swing performance Index: Developing a single-score index of golf swing rotational biomechanics quantified with 3D kinematics
references.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
references.establishes: Builds a single-score index on the professional benchmark curves, over 11 professionals and 5 amateurs spanning handicap 4 to novice. The selected formula combines three variables: peak pelvic rotational velocity before impact, pelvic rotational velocity AT IMPACT, and peak upper-torso rotational velocity after impact. Professionals standardise to 100 ± 10; amateurs average 82 ± 4. Independent support that pelvic rotational velocity at impact carries skill information.

references.title: Association between the On-Plane Angular Motions of the Axle-Chain System and Clubhead Speed in Skilled Male Golfers
references.authors: Madrid, Avalos, Levine, Tuttle, Becker, Kwon
references.establishes: 66 skilled golfers. Higher clubhead speed was associated with shorter downswings, larger rotation ranges, larger hip–shoulder separation at impact and delayed transitions — but clubhead speed was NOT well associated with wrist-cock angles or ranges, or with X-factor and X-factor stretch. This is the conflicting half of the wrist-release and X-factor claims; it is recorded here because it must be read, not because anything cites it.

references.title: Effects of on-plane wrist release style on morphological, temporal, and kinematic swing characteristic in golf drives performed by skilled male golfers
references.authors: Cheng, Mori, Lee, Martinez, Baek, Alvis, Kwon
references.establishes: 84 elite male golfers across four wrist-release styles. Delayed-release styles showed larger uncocking velocities, longer transitions, shorter early-downswing phases and a complete proximal-to-distal sequence, compared with early-release and recocking styles.

references.title: The Influence of Face Angle and Club Path on the Resultant Launch Angle of a Golf Ball
references.journal: Proceedings of the 12th Conference of the International Sports Engineering Association
references.establishes: Player and robot studies: initial launch direction falls 61–83% toward the face angle, with the remainder toward the club path, varying by club type.

references.title: The Role of Friction and Tangential Compliance on the Resultant Launch Angle of a Golf Ball
references.journal: Proceedings of the 13th Conference of the International Sports Engineering Association
references.establishes: A Hertzian impact model with tangential compliance via Coulomb friction predicts launch direction from delivered face angle and path, and explores launch direction against the friction coefficient.

references.title: The physics of golf
references.establishes: Peer-reviewed physics review: double-pendulum swing models, club–ball impact, the loft / launch / spin relationships, and turf interaction. The general impact physics behind most of the strike and ball-flight edges.

references.title: Small changes in ball position at address cause a chain effect in golf swing
references.authors: Kim, Lee, Lee, Lee, Shim, Lee
references.establishes: 20 professionals, five mediolateral ball positions, SPM analysis. Target-side ball position produced a significantly more open shoulder angle at address, during the downswing and at impact, plus lead-foot weight bias — and a less in-to-out club path at impact. The trend reversed for trail-side positions.

references.title: Biomechanical Effects of Ball Position on Address Position Variables of Elite Golfers
references.authors: Kim, Koh, Cho, Lee, Lee, Lee
references.journal: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
references.establishes: 11 male professional golfers, 3D motion analysis with eight infrared cameras and two force platforms, eight ball positions in the mediolateral and anteroposterior directions. Moving the ball mediolaterally significantly changed shoulder rotation and club-face aim at address and the vertical ground reaction force under the lead foot; at impact it significantly changed club-face aim, club path and angle of attack. The companion to Kim et al. 2021 — that one measures the address end, this one the delivery end. This journal issues no DOI, so the PMID is the identifier.

references.title: Towards a Biomechanical Understanding of Tempo in the Golf Swing
references.establishes: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed, and listed here for attribution rather than support. Models the body/club system as a simple harmonic oscillator — a biomechanical clock — accounting for total swing duration, the ratio of backswing to downswing time, and tempo's relative insensitivity to shot length. Shaft-mounted accelerometers at roughly 250 Hz, ten to twenty five-iron swings each, over 12 playing professionals, 13 teaching professionals and good amateurs, and 18 other golfers. The backswing:downswing ratio is centred at 3.0 in all three groups; playing professionals span 2.5 to 3.5 with very small per-golfer standard deviation and swing uniformly faster than the rest. This is the source of the widely quoted 3:1 figure. NOTE THE BASIS: their backswing is measured from the START OF MOTION, not from address, so it is not the same quantity this product's tempo ratio reports.

references.title: The role of biomechanics in maximising distance and accuracy of golf shots
references.establishes: Review of the biomechanics of distance and accuracy. General background; nothing in the pack cites it, and it is listed so a reader can find the survey rather than because a claim rests on it.
